1.pericope_label: At that time Merodachbaladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to Hezekiah: and Hezekiah was glad of them, and shewed them the house of his precious things. Then came Isaiah the prophet, and said, What said these men? and from whence came they unto thee?

schools.summary: Identifies the Babylonian king from the Assyrian monuments, reads the embassy as a political overture and the display of treasure as a showing of resources, and uses the treasury to date the visit.

Sifts the inherited identifications of the king, and reads the episode as a case study in the danger of prosperity, insisting that an act defensible at every point in appearance was corrupted at the root by ambition.

Compares the two copies of the history in detail and argues that a word has dropped out of both, and draws the moral lessons of the visit from both sides, the civility of the heathen and the interest behind it.
Turns the visit into a series of maxims on civility, on honouring those God honours, and on the difficulty of keeping the spirit low under great advancement.

positions.view: the Mardocempad of the astronomical canon, against the identifications with Nebuchadnezzar's father and with Esarhaddon, who ruled Assyria and not Babylon
a rebel against Sargon who set up an independent monarchy, styled son of Yakin in the inscriptions, which is probably a dynastic appellative
a vassal for twelve years who rebelled twice and ended a refugee on an island of the Persian Gulf
the first of his nation to bear the royal title, his father having governed without it, and the subduer of Assyria, so that it is a mistake to date that war from Nebuchadnezzar

genuine civility and religious awe at the sign given, which a heathen court could still turn to account, since the king made his court to Hezekiah not because he was pious but because he was prosperous

two ostensible objects, congratulation and enquiry about the sign on the dial, but really the opening of negotiations for an alliance, the present reading almost as an acknowledgment of Hezekiah's leadership in it
craft throughout: a pretence of congratulation meant to cajole, the heathen reckoning that an ally so visibly favoured by heaven would carry the war under heaven's protection

debates.question: Is the plea that the men came from a far country an excuse or a boast?

positions.view: an excuse: men who had travelled so far in his honour could hardly be refused, and a distant land seemed free of the danger of the Egyptian alliance
a boast, since the prophet knew the country well enough and needed no such magnificent language, which ambition supplied

outliers.reading: Compares the two copies of the history and judges that although the parallel account has hitherto been the more correct, here the advantage lies with this chapter, from which two of its words should be corrected; and argues from the Greek and from the later narration that a word for ambassadors has dropped out of both Hebrew copies, since the men are afterwards referred to as though they had been named already.

Reads the display of treasure as political rather than merely vain, a showing of the kingdom's resources to impress the ambassadors with Hezekiah's worth as an ally, and uses the state of the treasury to date the embassy before the payment made to the Assyrian.

themes: At that time Merodach–baladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to Hezekiah: for he had heard that he had been sick, and was recovered.

And Hezekiah was glad of them, and shewed them the house of his precious things, the silver, and the gold, and the spices, and the precious ointment, and all the house of his armour, and all that was found in his treasures: there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah shewed them not.

Then came Isaiah the prophet unto king Hezekiah, and said unto him, What said these men? and from whence came they unto thee? And Hezekiah said, They are come from a far country unto me, even from Babylon.
Then said he, What have they seen in thine house? And Hezekiah answered, All that is in mine house have they seen: there is nothing among my treasures that I have not shewed them.

5.pericope_label: Then said Isaiah to Hezekiah, Hear the word of the Lord of hosts: behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house shall be carried to Babylon. Then said Hezekiah, Good is the word of the Lord which thou hast spoken; for there shall be peace and truth in my days

schools.summary: Judges the king's reply less true and noble than a comparable confession elsewhere, and glosses the second word of his hope as stability.

Argues from the severity of the sentence back to the gravity of the fault, sets out and dismisses every apology the act admits of, defends the reply as gratitude for a mitigation, and answers the objection that a nation's captivity cannot be charged to one man.
Divides between a reading that rescues the king by taking his last words as a question and a set of maxims drawing the retributive fitness of the punishment.
Reads the sentence as exactly answering the sin and allows the king a reasonable contentment in the peace of his own days.

debates.question: What does the king's reply mean?

positions.view: immediate repentance: the sin acknowledged, the sentence owned as just, and mercy seen in the delay
resignation less true and noble than the confession of a king who asked what the sheep had done, and a thanksgiving recalling too much the saying that after him may come the flood

not a statement but a humble question, whether there shall be prosperity in his days and whether he shall escape the evil foretold; understood otherwise the words show a pitiful unconcern for his family and nation

gratitude for a mitigation: the particle marks an exception, so he thanks God for delaying what might have fallen at once, and the profane sayings that wish the earth burnt after one's death are quite a different thing
a reasonable contentment: we must not be regardless of those who come after, yet may count it a favour to reach harbour before the storm

debates.question: How does the sentence fit the sin?

positions.view: the severity proves the fault no ordinary one, since God observes the highest moderation in chastising, and men judge amiss where God alone is competent
it is exactly retributive, taking from him what he made the matter of his pride, as a traveller who displays his gold to one who proves a thief
it is just, with mercy mixed in, since time was given and the sentence not executed at once

outliers.reading: Raises against himself the objection that a city's sack and a nation's captivity cannot justly be charged to one man, since scripture elsewhere lays them to the people's general obstinacy, and answers that God may punish one man's sin and a whole nation's crimes at once, so that no man throws the blame on others; citing the numbering of the people, where the anger of the Lord was kindled against the nation first and the king's act followed.
Dates the fulfilment about a hundred and fifty years after the words were spoken and calls the interval a proof of divine omniscience, where the others expect it within a few reigns.

themes: Then said Isaiah to Hezekiah, Hear the word of the Lord of hosts:
Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store until this day, shall be carried to Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the Lord.
And of thy sons that shall issue from thee, which thou shalt beget, shall they take away; and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.
Then said Hezekiah to Isaiah, Good is the word of the Lord which thou hast spoken. He said moreover, For there shall be peace and truth in my days.
